To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

p53 mutations occur in 66% of human breast carcinoma cell line, that the p53 muta-tional status correlates with the copy number of p53, that the extent of p53 mRNA and protein expression varies considerably in the different human breast carcinoma cell, and that p53 mutations are associated with aneuploidy in these cells.

the DNA content of 24 human breast cancer cell lines ranged between 0.85 and 2.58 and that 16 cell lines contained mutated p53 alleles, 13 of which expressed only the mutated and three both the wild-type and the mutated alleles.

(i) the p53 mutation status in human breast cancer cell lines can be assessed by a functional yeast assay, (ii) this assay is highly sensitive and specific and (iii) the p53 mRNA and protein expression levels in breast cancer cell lines vary considerably.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of p53 gene mutations, expression and function in human breast carcinoma cell cultures.
the p53 gene and its product, the p53 protein.

the development and application of a new method for the analysis of gene expression, which is based on the detection of mRNA and protein expression by competitive reverse transcription-pulverase chain reaction and immunocytochemical analysis, respectively.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
p53 mutations are present in 16 of the 24 breast carcinoma cell lines studied and that the extent of mRNA and protein expression is not necessarily related to the mutational status of this gene.
, at the moment, there is no reliable method to detect p53 mutations.
the p53 status is not a major factor for the growth and/or survival of the majority of the breast carcinoma cell lines analyzed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the p53 mutaional status is not necessarily reflected in the expression level of the p53 gene.
p53 mutation status, mRNA and p53 protein expression levels in breast cancer cell lines are not correlated.

the FISH and the FASAY methods were very useful in the detection of p53 gene alterations, and that the immunocytochemical and the western blot methods were very useful to detect p53 protein expression.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the p53 mutaional status is not necessarily reflected in the mRNA and/or protein expression levels.
the p53 muta-tional status is not necessarily reflected in its respective mRNA and/or protein levels.
the p53 mutaional status is the most important determinant of its expression in breast carcinoma cell lines, and that the p53 mRNA and protein expression levels are highly variable.
